Your DISCO's full bill with fixed charge, taxes and FPA: [[F2|LESCO]], [[F3|IESCO]], [[F4|MEPCO]], [[F5|GEPCO]], [[F6|FESCO]], [[F7|PESCO]], [[F8|HESCO]], [[F9|SEPCO]], [[F10|QESCO]], [[F11|TESCO]], [[F12|K-Electric]].

fields.name: import_units
fields.label: Units imported from the grid
fields.hint: Units taken from the grid in the month, from your bill (the import or consumption reading).

fields.name: export_units
fields.label: Units exported to the grid
fields.hint: Units your solar system sent to the grid in the month, from the export reading on the bill.

fields.name: buyback_rs
fields.label: Buyback rate
fields.hint: Rs per exported unit: NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}, the rate the Prosumer Regulations use. News in {{data.tariff.net_billing.reported_when}} quoted about {{data.tariff.net_billing.reported_rs_per_unit|rs}} a unit, a figure under discussion that NEPRA did not notify. If your agreement or DISCO credits another rate, type it here; you can try both.

fields.name: sanctioned_kw
fields.label: Sanctioned load
fields.hint: From your bill. At {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more the import is billed on Time-of-Use (peak and off-peak) rates: enter the peak units below. For the whole ToU bill with fixed charge, surcharges and GST use the [[F13|ToU bill calculator]].

fields.name: peak_units
fields.label: Units imported in peak hours (ToU)
fields.hint: Only for a sanctioned load of {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more: the peak import units on your ToU bill. Blank uses our estimate of {{d.tou_peak_share|pct}} of the import.

fields.name: protected
fields.label: Protected consumer (all of the last six months under the protected limit)
fields.hint: Tick only if every one of your last six bills was within the protected unit limit. Not at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more.

fields.name: before_units
fields.label: Units a month before solar
fields.hint: For the saving and the payback: the units of an average month before you had solar (a year's units divided by twelve is best). It cannot be less than the units you import now.

fields.name: system_rs
fields.label: Solar system price
fields.hint: The installed price on your quote. No quote yet? The [[D14|solar system price estimate]] gives a typical price for your size.

outputs.label: Net bill under net billing, energy only
Same month under old net metering
Extra you pay under net billing
Saving a month against no solar

answer: A home that imports {{in.import_units|int}} units and exports {{in.export_units|int}} units pays about {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} in energy charges under net billing, against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} under old net metering, so net billing costs {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more that month. Net bill = imported units × slab rate − exported units × buyback rate of {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}}.
how: Import: {{out.import_calc}} = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}. Export credit: {{out.export_units}} units × {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} = {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}. Net billing energy charge = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}} − {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} = {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}; any credit above the import bill carries forward ({{out.carry_forward_rs|rs}} here). Old net metering: {{out.nm_calc}} = {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}. Difference = {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}}. Fixed charges, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST are added on top; use the bill calculator for the full bill (the ToU bill calculator at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more). {{out.payback_calc}}
key_facts: Under net billing the imported units are billed at the normal slab rate ({{out.import_rate|rs2}} per unit for {{out.import_units|int}} units) and exported units are bought back at a flat rate, {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit, NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}.

Under old net metering exported units cancelled imported units one for one, so a home importing {{out.import_units|int}} and exporting {{out.export_units|int}} units paid for only {{out.net_metering_units|int}} units, at the lower slab those units reach ({{out.net_metering_rate|rs2}}).

For the same {{out.import_units|int}} imported and {{out.export_units|int}} exported units, net billing charges {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} and old net metering {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}: a difference of {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} a month in energy charges alone.
The net billing figure is energy charges only; the fixed charge per sanctioned kW, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST are added on the real bill.

formula.text: Net billing Rs = max(0, import × slab rate − export × buyback); old net metering Rs = max(0, import − export) × slab rate of the net units
lines: import = units taken from the grid in the month
export = units sent to the grid in the month
slab rate = unprotected (or protected) A-1 rate of the band the units reach
buyback = flat Rs per exported unit under net billing
Credit larger than the import bill carries forward to the next month
Extra = net billing Rs − old net metering Rs, never below zero

sections.h2: Net metering calculator vs net billing: what changed in 2026?
p: Under the old net metering rules a bidirectional meter counted units in and units out, and the DISCO billed only the difference. Every exported unit cancelled an imported unit at the same slab rate, and if you exported more than you imported the spare units carried forward to the next month.

Under the NEPRA Prosumer Regulations notified in 2026, new solar connections are on net billing. Imports are billed at the normal slab rate of the band your imported units reach, and exports are bought at a flat buyback rate that is far below the slab rate. The two numbers are worked out separately and then set against each other, which is why the same month costs more under net billing.

Agreements signed before {{data.tariff.net_billing.existing_cutoff}} keep the rate and rules of the old net-metering regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; renewals move to net billing. Ask your DISCO when your agreement ends.

sections.h2: How is a net metering bill calculated in Pakistan?
p: Old rules: net units = imported − exported. If the result is positive, those net units are billed at the slab they reach, exactly like a home without solar. If the result is negative, the bill for energy is zero and the spare units are credited to the next month. For the default month above that gives {{out.net_metering_units|int}} net units at {{out.net_metering_rate|rs2}} = {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}.

New rules (net billing): imported units × slab rate gives the import bill, {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}} for {{out.import_units|int}} units here. Exported units × buyback rate gives the credit, {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} for {{out.export_units|int}} units. Bill = import bill − credit = {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}. Because all imported units are charged at the slab their total reaches, exporting does not pull you into a lower slab any more.

sections.h2: What is the net billing rate for solar exports in Pakistan?
p: The calculator uses {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per exported unit. The {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, credit exported units at the national average energy purchase price, and NEPRA's power purchase price decision for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}} puts that price at {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}}. NEPRA sets it again for each year and may revise it by notification, so change the buyback field if your bill shows a different rate.

Compare that with the import rate of {{out.import_rate|rs2}} per unit for {{out.import_units|int}} units: a unit you export is worth a fraction of a unit you import. Using your own solar power in the day, running the water pump, washing machine and AC while the sun is up, is worth more than exporting it; check [[N6|how much your panels will make tomorrow]] to plan those loads for the sunniest hours.

sections.h2: Does excess export still carry forward?
p: Yes, in rupees rather than units. If the export credit for the month is larger than the import bill, the bill for energy is zero and the spare credit carries forward to the next month. The calculator shows the carry-forward amount instead of a negative bill. Under old net metering it was spare units that carried forward.

examples.title: Import {{in.import_units|int}} units, export {{in.export_units|int}} units, and the payback
examples.text: Import bill {{out.import_units|int}} × {{out.import_rate|rs2}} ({{out.import_band}} slab) = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}; export credit {{out.export_units|int}} × {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} = {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}; net billing charge {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}. Old net metering billed {{out.net_metering_units|int}} net units at {{out.net_metering_rate|rs2}} = {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}, so net billing costs {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more. Before solar the home used {{in.before_units|int}} units, an energy charge of {{out.before_energy_rs|rs}}; net billing saves {{out.monthly_saving_rs|rs}} a month, {{out.yearly_saving_rs|rs}} a year, so a {{in.system_rs|rs}} system pays back in {{out.payback_years|1}} years on energy charges alone, before any change in tariff or panel output.

examples.title: Export more than you import: {{in.import_units|int}} in, {{in.export_units|int}} out
examples.text: Import bill {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}} at {{out.import_rate|rs2}} a unit ({{out.import_band}} slab); export credit {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}. Net billing still leaves {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} to pay, because the credit per exported unit is lower than the cost per imported unit. Under old net metering the energy bill was {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} and {{out.net_metering_carry_units|int}} units carried forward.

examples.title: Credit larger than the import bill: {{in.import_units|int}} in, {{in.export_units|int}} out
examples.text: Import bill {{out.import_units|int}} × {{out.import_rate|rs2}} ({{out.import_band}} slab) = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}; export credit {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}. The energy charge is {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} and {{out.carry_forward_rs|rs}} of credit carries forward to next month. Under old net metering {{out.net_metering_carry_units|int}} spare units would have carried forward instead.

examples.title: Protected consumer: {{in.import_units|int}} in, {{in.export_units|int}} out
examples.text: A protected home is billed slab-wise at the protected rates up to {{out.import_rate|rs2}} in the {{out.import_band}} protected slab, so the import bill is {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}. The export credit is {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} and the net billing charge {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}, against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} for {{out.net_metering_units|int}} net units under old net metering: {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more. The gap is small because protected rates are close to the buyback rate.

examples.title: ToU meter, {{in.sanctioned_kw|int}} kW: {{in.import_units|int}} in ({{in.peak_units|int}} in peak hours), {{in.export_units|int}} out
examples.text: At {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more the import is billed on peak and off-peak rates: {{out.import_calc}} = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}; export credit {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}; net billing charge {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}. Solar exports happen in daylight, which is off-peak, so old net metering netted them against the off-peak import only: {{out.nm_calc}} = {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}. Net billing costs {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more. Without the peak units from your bill, the tool assumes {{d.tou_peak_share|pct}} of the import falls in peak hours, an estimate.

mistakes: Subtracting exports from imports first. Under net billing all imported units are billed at the slab their total reaches; only the rupee credit is subtracted afterwards.
Treating this as the full bill. The result is the energy charge only; the fixed charge, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST come on top and are worked out by the bill calculator.
Using the buyback rate as a fixed fact. It is an estimate until NEPRA or your DISCO publishes it; enter the rate from your own bill.
Ticking protected when a single month in the last six went over the limit. One high month moves you to unprotected rates for every unit.
safety: Only a AEDB-certified installer and a licensed electrician may connect a solar system for export, and the bidirectional meter is installed by the DISCO; never bypass the meter or back-feed the grid through a plug socket.

faq.q: What is the net billing calculation for a solar home?
faq.a: Imported units × the slab rate they reach, minus exported units × the buyback rate. For {{out.import_units|int}} imported and {{out.export_units|int}} exported units that is {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}} − {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} = {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} in energy charges.

faq.q: What is the solar export rate in Pakistan?
faq.a: {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}: the national average energy purchase price in NEPRA's power purchase price decision, which the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, use for exported units. Under old net metering exported units first cancelled imported ones unit for unit.

faq.q: Why do some sites say {{data.tariff.net_billing.reported_rs_per_unit|rs}} a unit for exported solar units?
faq.a: News reports in {{data.tariff.net_billing.reported_when}} quoted a buyback of about {{data.tariff.net_billing.reported_rs_per_unit|rs}} a unit that was under discussion; NEPRA did not notify it (Express Tribune report in Sources), and some sites still quote it. NEPRA's power purchase price decision for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}} sets the national average energy purchase price at {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}}, and that is the rate the Prosumer Regulations use for exported units. If your agreement or DISCO credits a different rate, type it in the buyback box and compare both results.

faq.q: How much does a solar home save under net metering compared with net billing?
faq.a: For the default month, old net metering charged {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} and net billing charges {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}, so net metering saved {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more. Savings against having no solar at all are larger under both, because every unit you use in the day is not bought at all.

faq.q: Is there a solar payback calculator for Pakistan?
faq.a: Yes, on this page. Enter your monthly units before solar and the system price: the saving is the energy charge of those units without solar minus the net billing charge, and payback in years is the price divided by twelve months of that saving. A home that used {{ex.0.in.before_units|int}} units a month before solar and now imports {{ex.0.in.import_units|int}} and exports {{ex.0.in.export_units|int}} saves {{ex.0.out.monthly_saving_rs|rs}} a month, so a {{ex.0.in.system_rs|rs}} system pays back in {{ex.0.out.payback_years|1}} years. The saving counts energy charges only; GST and the other per-unit lines on the units you no longer buy make the real payback shorter.

faq.q: Does the buyback rate for solar change?
faq.a: Yes. It is the national average energy purchase price, which NEPRA sets for each year and may revise by notification. If your bill shows a different rate, enter it in the buyback field.

faq.q: How are net metering units calculated on the bill?
faq.a: The bidirectional meter has an import reading and an export reading. Under old net metering the DISCO billed import minus export; under net billing the two readings are priced separately and set against each other in rupees. This calculator accepts both readings and shows both results.

faq.q: Can I still apply for net metering in 2026?
faq.a: New connections under the Prosumer Regulations are on net billing. Agreements signed before {{data.tariff.net_billing.existing_cutoff}} keep the rate and rules of the old net-metering regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; renewals move to net billing.
